input.title: Stages 8–10 are designed but unshipped: sync serving withholds whole scope runs per poll and holds rather than consumes them, the permission tables migrate into ordered grant lists, then the host stops consulting them

input.description: Serving never withholds auth/document scopes and intersects with the host check; channels bind to a subject by adoption. Migration: one INITIALIZE_AUTH per document; untranslatable rows are refused.

metadata.reason: Extracted from docs/specs/auth-scope.md at v6.2.2-dev.74 — Reads (serving, per-poll subject); Stage 8; Stage 9; Stage 10
Picks up where the shipped stages stop and records the designed remainder

input.content:
Design intent as of v6.2.2-dev.74 — nothing in this note has shipped.

**Stage 8 — the serving path (`authEnforcement`).** `pollSyncEnvelopes` withholds scopes the polling subject may not read, instead of asking the host's tables which whole documents to drop. Three rules make that safe. *Whole runs only*: an outbox entry is one `(document, scope, branch)` run; withholding part of one is silent corruption, because the receiving executor renumbers arriving operations against its own head and validates no hashes. *Hold, never consume*: the present filter marks a refused entry delivered and the acknowledgement trim evicts it irreversibly — and a channel has no identity, so a subject polling while logged out would evict operations its logged-in identity was owed; held entries cost memory instead, the persisted cursor never advances past the lowest unserved entry, and a capped outbox evicts newest-first without marking delivered. *The metadata scopes are never withheld*, so a peer can always reach the decision the origin reached. The verdict is **intersected** with the host's existing check, never unioned, which is what makes it safe before migration. Because the subject is per poll and possibly absent, a channel comes to belong to a subject **by adoption**: created authenticated it is bound at once; created anonymously it serves what the policy serves anonymous callers until the first authenticated poll claims it, after which polls under another address are refused with the shape of a read denial.

**Stage 9 — migrating the tables (no flag).** The tables are the fleet's live access control and every existing auth scope is empty, so enforcement cannot turn on until the tables are grants. A migration submits one `INITIALIZE_AUTH` per document through the executor (grants are event-sourced; it cannot write rows) with an **ordered** list in which each step claws back what the previous one granted too widely: READ rows → allow read `*`; WRITE rows → allow read and execute `*`; restricted operations → deny `{anyone}` then re-allow the named addresses; then deny `{anyone}` execute on `auth`; then owner and ADMIN rows → read and execute `*`. Reclaiming by order rather than enumerating scopes keeps a scope added later covered. Every migrated policy must name an explicit `execute`-on-`auth` administrator, because no existing document has a signed header. What has no faithful translation — inherited protection, more than 100 principals, node-local administrators — is refused and reported, never approximated; migrating also publishes every access list to every replica, accepted rather than mitigated. It runs on one replica with auth writes quiesced and is idempotent.

**Stage 10 — retiring the tables (`authEnforcement`).** The host stops consulting them on the read path; the auth scope becomes the only read authorization, while the host's own closed-by-default setting survives as one read-surface setting. A reactor refuses to boot with `authEnforcement` on while untranslated rows remain (unless the host closes by default), and listings keep dropping whole documents rather than leaking ids, slugs and names.

_Source: docs/specs/auth-scope.md (Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.74)._
